extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, political scientists, journalism researchers, and journalists interested in newsworthiness and agenda-setting
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria for what makes political events or topics newsworthy under Cook's institutional frame, and how the press functions as a political institution that co-produces policy. Useful for analyzing news selection, agenda-setting, and press-government interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as a political institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The press should be understood as an institution that coproduces policy alongside government rather than merely reporting on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has standardized routines (beats, deadlines, formats); shared professional norms across outlets; collective power exceeding any single outlet's intentions; and the capacity to set which issues officials must address. Use this frame to treat news selection as a negotiation between newsworkers and political actors driven by institutional incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized-Version Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reporters base coverage on high-level government sources, news presents an 'authorized version' reflecting what officials need to have reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect stories that privilege official narratives and sanctioned accounts; coverage will often mirror the versions officials craft for public consumption. Analysts should look for reliance on high-level sources as a sign of this premium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-Reporter Symbiosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials need coverage to advance agendas; reporters need access. Stories that serve both interests get told most readily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pieces for mutual benefit between source and reporter (e.g., trial balloons, controlled leaks, mutually useful scoops). Such mutual-serving stories are disproportionately likely to appear and to receive follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-arranged Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials craft events (speeches, ceremonies, press conferences) for media; the staging itself produces newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that staged events pass predictability and visual-newsworthiness tests; the existence of a press-oriented setup often suffices for coverage regardless of substantive novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-Outlet Convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The news institution operates collectively; what is treated as news at one major outlet tends to be treated as news at others by professional convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rapid copying or mutual reinforcement across outlets (e.g., NYT, WaPo, major broadcast networks). Convergence reflects institutional norms and reduces heterogeneity of what counts as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional Self-Reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the press as institution declares an issue newsworthy, the political system responds (officials speak, hearings convene), generating more news — a closed loop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track feedback loops where media attention begets official activity that begets more media attention. Issue trajectories can be self-sustaining due to this reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue Surfacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Press attention forces officials to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether media visibility elevates a previously ignored problem onto the political agenda; surfacing is a primary mechanism of media influence on policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Press framing fixes the terms of subsequent debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how journalistic frames constrain policy discourse by defining problems, acceptable solutions, and the actors involved. Early frames often persist and shape later policy deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue Persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Press follow-up sustains issues; press abandonment kills them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure persistence by continued coverage and follow-up stories; recognize that institutionalized beats and routines make some issues durable while others fade quickly when coverage stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution Pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Press demand for closure shapes policy decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cases where media timelines or calls for decisive action pressure policymakers toward particular resolutions or accelerated decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability Pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing press attention disciplines officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ongoing scrutiny as a constraint on official behavior and as a mechanism creating incentives for transparency, resignations, or policy change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional Beat Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the press is institutionalized, coverage is also institutionalized: White House, Congress, Treasury, Pentagon, State each have permanent press corps. Newsworthiness is heavily skewed toward these beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect systematic coverage advantage for topics with established beats; topics lacking a beat struggle to sustain coverage. Use existence of a dedicated press corps as predictor of topic salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbiotic Story Premium (for selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that serve both reporter and source interests (e.g., trial-balloon leaks, scoops on insider battles) achieve disproportionate coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding stories, flag those that provide advantages to both journalists (access, scoops) and sources (agenda advancement, messaging). These are more likely to be selected and amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-Setup Events
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies, anniversaries, photo ops are inherently newsworthy because they are designed for the press; they pass the predictability and visual newsworthiness tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate staged events as pre-packaged content that meets newsroom routines; visual and predictable elements increase selection odds independent of substantive policy content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-Outlet Solidarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The press defends its access collectively; stories that defend press freedom (e.g., subpoena fights) get cross-outlet coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unified coverage when the institutional interests of the press are at stake; such solidarity reflects collective institutional incentives beyond single-outlet considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel Changes as Newsworthy Signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet appointments, hires, fires are highly newsworthy because they affect the press's institutional access patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat personnel events as structurally important signals that alter beat access and the flow of information; these attract coverage because they reconfigure institutional relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way co-production of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness is not just what newsrooms select but what the press-government system collectively constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt analytic perspectives that account for mutual construction: both news organizations and political actors shape what becomes news through interaction and negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction of institutional inertia
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthy topics tend to persist because the institutional infrastructure (beat reporters, press offices) keeps producing material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of institutional infrastructure around a topic to predict its staying power; lack of infrastructure suggests difficulty achieving sustained coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability of topic salience
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic salience can be predicted from the existence of institutional press apparatus around a topic; non-institutionalized topics struggle for sustained coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For empirical work, operationalize salience measures by coding the presence/strength of beats, press offices, and routine coverage practices tied to specific policy areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging newsroom sociology and political-institutional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Cook's framework links Tuchman/Fishman-style newsroom sociology (routines, norms) with political-institutional analysis (how institutions shape policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply combined lenses: interpret newsroom practices in light of institutional incentives and evaluate political outcomes as co-produced by media institutions and government actors.
